<reason>Both sides were skilled and disciplined (no fake sourcing, clean Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 compliance), and A arguably out-executed B in rebuttal craft: A2.1 punctured B's "your fixes ARE the motion" hijack by distinguishing reason-triggered requests from an age-keyed default, A2.5's water-bill flip answered the bathroom analogy, A4 split B's Q2 dilemma (partial vs. full concealment), and A5 directly inverted B's closing frame ("only half the silence"). A also plainly won the billing-accountability sub-clash. But B's central mechanism — deterrence means the realistic alternative is no treatment, and the frightened cannot opt into privacy they don't know exists — survived as the debate's gravitational center. A's mitigation ("the generic envelope can't hurt her") sat in unresolved tension with A's own insistence that intake-triggered confidentiality is needed, and B's means-tested-coverage answer (B4.1–B4.2) to A's severability point was never squarely re-engaged. B's capability-asymmetry frame ("put the burden on the confident, not the terrified") remained the cleanest decision rule on the table. The margin stays small because B was clipped twice and B's closing recap'd its frame without answering A's escalated "disappearance" characterization, while A adapted well and got the last word.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was B2.2–B2.3 ("CON spent a speech describing how to implement the motion, then voted against it") against A2.1's riposte (a request is triggered by reason; the motion is concealment by default keyed to nothing but age, deciding "who is protected and who silently pays"). That clash reset the whole debate onto defaults and error-asymmetry, which both closings then fought over.</best_rebuttal>
